Before we begin this evening's meeting, I'd like to take a moment to recognize several important days being observed during the month of May,
including Canadian Jewish Heritage Month, Asian Heritage Month, Polish Heritage Month, and Croatian Heritage Month.
Together, these observances give us an opportunity to celebrate the rich histories, cultures, and contributions of communities that have long helped shape Kitchener and Canada.
In fact, we just had the Polish community gathering outside at the corner of Duke and Young for the raising of the Polish flag for their Constitution Day.
Canadian Jewish Heritage Month recognizes the history, culture and contributions of Jewish communities across the country.
For generations, Jewish Canadians have strengthened our cultural life, our economy and our public institutions, including right here in Kitchener.
Asian Heritage Month provides an opportunity to reflect on the diversity, resilience and contribution of people and communities of Asian heritage.
Asian Canadians continue to play a vital role in shaping our city and our country
through leadership, entrepreneurship, arts and culture, and community service.
Polish and Croatian Heritage Months allow us to celebrate the traditions, stories,
and lasting contributions of Polish and Croatian Canadians
whose communities are an important part of Kitchener's social, cultural, and economic fabric.
This month also recognizes National Youth Month,
a time to celebrate the contributions of young people in our community
as well as the important role they play in shaping Kitchener's future.
And later this month, we'll be acknowledging them through the Kayak Youth Awards.
Later this month, we will also observe Public Works Week,
which honors the essential work of our public works professionals
who help keep our city safe, connected, and running every day,
often behind the scenes and in all conditions 24-7, 365.
We're also observing Mental Health Awareness Week beginning on today, May the 4th.
This week is an opportunity to recognize the importance of mental health, reduce stigma, and encourage open conversations about well-being.
May 5th also marks Red Dress Day, a national day of remembrance in action that honors missing and murdered Indigenous women, girls, and two-spirit people.
The red dress serves as a powerful symbol and reminder of calling attention to lives lost, families affected, and the ongoing need for awareness, truth, and meaningful action.

Together, these observances remind us of the strength of our diversity, the importance of inclusion, and the shared responsibility we all have to ensure everyone in our community feels valued and that they belong.

And so on behalf of the Council, staff, and all of us at the City of Kitchener, I acknowledge these important observances and thank members of our community who help make our city a more inclusive and welcoming place for all.
We also want to take a moment to recognize that May 3rd to 9th is Emergency Preparedness Week in Canada.
Emergency Preparedness Week is a national effort led by Public Safety Canada,
provincial and territorial emergency management organizations, municipalities,
Indigenous organizations, non-governmental organizations, and private sector companies.
This week, we encourage people in Canada to take concrete actions
to be better prepared to protect themselves and their households during emergencies.
Working independently and in close collaboration with our regional partners,
the City of Kitchener is prepared to manage emergencies that may impact the safety of our community.
We are all strongest when we work together, so both this week and year-round,

The Share the Road Cycling Coalition
is Ontario's cycling advocacy and policy organization
created in 2007 to unite cycling organizations
from across the province,

to enhance their ability to be more bicycle-friendly,

The awards recognize municipalities across Ontario
that have demonstrated exceptional commitment
creating safe, accessible, and vibrant cycling cultures and communities.
Municipalities who apply receive an in-depth report that honors their success
and progress and provides practical information on how to focus investments

satisfaction of responding to residents, to people who want to ride more often,

across five key areas, engineering, education, encouragement, equity and planning, and evaluation.
Awards are granted at bronze, silver, gold, and platinum levels, reflecting a community's
commitment to improving conditions for cyclists and fostering a vibrant cycling culture.
In December, we announced eight more award winners, bringing the total number of bicycle-friendly
communities in Ontario to 61, representing more than 10.8 million residents, or nearly
two-thirds of Ontario's population. There are a number of attributes that bike-friendly
communities have, things like a connected network and grid, connections to transit,
safe places for people to ride, opportunities for economic development through tourism,
all of which Kitchener has. Bicycle-friendly municipalities exemplify innovation and dedication
to creating a healthy, safe and active community with important investments in cycling infrastructure,
cycling education programs and community engagement initiatives. The City of
Kitchener joins a growing network of bicycle-friendly communities across
